(This evening through next Monday)
Issued at 1224 PM CDT Tue Oct 13 2026

Morning upper air analysis places an amplifying ridge over the
Gulf coastline in Texas and east into the southeastern CONUS with
a trough centered over Nevada. In response to increasing upper
heights, surface temperatures will continue to remain at record
levels through Thursday, climbing into the low to mid 90s. In
addition to the heat, southerlies have begun to advect higher
moisture north and east into the Ohio River Valley, leading to
heat indices near 100 F along and west of the Mississippi River.
Instability will begin to increase as well this afternoon with
MUCAPE values increasing to around 1000  - 1500 J/kg. Observed
soundings and forecast soundings alike show an uncapped air mass,
which would allow for isolated convection. However, most CAMs do
not initiate any convection today, likely due to a lack of
sustained low-level convergence. So, showers and thunderstorms
are unlikely through Tuesday.

Wednesday will be a different story with increasing shower and
thunderstorm chances ahead of a stalling cold front. A cold front
will sag south through Tuesday and much of Wednesday, eventually
stalling just north of the Mid-South. Moisture will continue to
be advected in advance of the boundary and will keep the moderate
instability from Tuesday throughout the region. Thunderstorms are
expected to develop along and south of the boundary. Forecast
soundings indicate that effective wind shear values will be quite
weak at a paltry 15 - 20 knots. This will lead to unorganized,
mostly single-cell thunderstorm structures capable of gusty
winds. PWATs are forecast to surpass 2.00" within the moisture
axis, which is well above the 95th percentile for this time of
year. Therefore, rainfall within thunderstorms will be heavy and
could produce localized flooding issues. Storm motions above
15 knots and dry ground will keep a higher flooding threat at
bay, but an east-west oriented stationary boundary could lead to
training thunderstorms which could locally increase flash
flooding potential, especially across the northern third of the
CWA.

Surface high pressure to the east of the region will begin to
move farther east into Thursday. Moisture that will be present is
then forecast to advect north with drier air in the wake of
Isaias over the gulf being advected into the region. This is
expected to dramatically decrease precipitation coverage
throughout the region through Thursday. In the meantime, a trough
will begin to amplify over the Midwest, throwing a strong cold
front south across the central CONUS. The cold front will arrive
at the Mid-South Friday with blustery winds, cooler air, and,
thanks to the removal of moisture, dry conditions. Highs on
Friday will therefore mark a significant change relative to the
rest of this week with highs in the 60s and 70s for the majority
of the region. Similar weather will persist through the weekend.
Lows will also fall into the 40s Saturday and Sunday mornings
with a 30% - 40% chance for portions of West Tennessee to fall
into the 30s Sunday morning.

Another aspect to the forecast, especially through this weekend,
will be enhanced fire danger potential. Ahead of and just behind
the cold front, winds will become sustained between 15 - 25 mph
with gusts above 30 mph expected. Much of the region remains in
D2 (Severe) and D3 (Extreme) drought, keeping fuels 1-hour and 10-
hour fuels dry. This would lead to the potential for fires to
spread in the absence of higher surface dewpoints with forecast
relative humidity values around or below 30% late Friday and
Saturday. Therefore, a Rangeland Fire Danger Statement may be
required Friday with SPC placing a 40% Critical outline for areas
along the Mississippi River. For now, Red Flag Warnings are not
anticipated due to minimum relative humidity values below 25%
remaining isolated, but guidance at this range often
underestimates the degree of mixing. So, lower relative humidity
values could enter the forecast over a larger area through the
end of the week and is worth monitoring in future forecast
updates.

An upper ridge axis will move east from the Plains and into the
Mississippi River Valley by the end of the weekend. NBM guidance
produces a gradual warming trend into next week, but
deterministic guidance still seems to have run-to-run
inconsistencies regarding the surface pattern. So, cooler
temperatures and dry weather could last longer into next week.
For now, expect average, fall-like weather to end the forecast
period with the expectation for a warming trend late next week.
